clue.text: A column, article in French, writing that defines religious beliefs

definitions.text: A column, article in French, writing that defines religious beliefs

parts.note: a post is an upright pillar or column
les is the French plural definite article, 'the'
a creed is a formal written statement of what a church believes

explanation.surface: Someone describes a newspaper column and a French article as a document setting out a faith.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the pieces build the answer, and read together they also describe the statement of faith named after the twelve followers of Christ.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the traditional Christian statement of faith, a short summary of core doctrine recited in church services.

clue.text: Preconceived idea of what trip might be into foreign capital

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are placed into the middle of the city name

parts.note: Paris is the capital of France, foreign to a British setter

indicators.note: what the word trip 'might be' asks for another arrangement of its four letters

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what a holiday trip to a foreign capital might turn out to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' asks what the word could become rearranged; 'of' is a link, and 'foreign' only tells a British solver the capital is abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: This French phrase means a view formed in advance, a prejudice or bias held before considering the facts.

clue.text: Otherworldly type isn't for following society

indicators.note: the informal word for isn't comes after the abbreviation for society

parts.note: ain't is the colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A dreamy, unworldly person is described as someone who doesn't go along with society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts AINT after S; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A holy person is thought of as devoted to spiritual rather than worldly matters, an otherworldly figure.

clue.text: No fellow for mixing

indicators.note: the letters of the two words no fellow are put up for mixing into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is described as having no companion to socialise with.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of NO FELLOW rearrange into the answer, and the whole clue also describes such a person: someone with no friend to mix with.
explanation.definitionFit: A solitary person who prefers to act alone is someone with no companion and no wish to socialise.

clue.text: Perverse pleasure of hell embraced by little man

indicators.note: the word for hell is held inside the short name, as if hugged

parts.note: Sam is a shortened form of Samuel, a man's name made little
Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and Dante's name for the city of hell

explanation.surface: A small man is gripped by a hellish, twisted enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: Dis is a Roman name for the underworld god, and Dante's city of hell in the Inferno; 'little man' means a man's name in its short form. 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the taking of pleasure in inflicting pain or cruelty, a perverse kind of enjoyment.

clue.text: Tall structure — notice one in a storm moving

indicators.note: the notice and the numeral go inside the rearranged letters
the letters of a storm are set moving into a new order

parts.note: ad, short for advertisement, is a notice
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A tall structure is seen with a notice on it in a moving storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges A STORM into ROMAST; 'in' puts AD and I inside it after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcasting mast is a tall upright structure carrying aerials for transmitting signals.

clue.text: Troublemakers blocking hotel vestibule

indicators.note: the answer sits across the two words, blocking the gap between them

explanation.surface: Mischief-makers are standing in a hotel lobby, blocking the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across hotEL VEStibule.
explanation.definitionFit: In folklore these little sprites play mischievous tricks on people, making trouble.

clue.text: Avoid possibility of loose tile and settle down domestically

definitions.meaning: tile is old slang for a hat; putting it on a hook means it can't be knocked loose
the idiom means to make a home somewhere, settling into domestic life

explanation.surface: Someone guards against a slipping roof tile and settles into home life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tile' looks like a roof tile, but it is old British slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally storing your headgear on a peg, and idiomatically taking up residence and settling down at home.

clue.text: Maybe I fix ordinance

parts.note: I is an example of a part of speech that stands for a noun, hence 'maybe'
to cement is to fix firmly in place

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they could perhaps fix a regulation themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker, but it is a word being classified: I is a pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an official decree, and an authoritative declaration is a formal announcement of that kind.

clue.text: A king and what he did, we hear, to get accused

parts.note: R, for rex, is the abbreviation for king

indicators.note: signals that the words what he did are replaced by a word that sounds like a different spelling

parts.note: a king reigned, ruling over his country

explanation.surface: A king and what he did are described as being charged with a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: REIGNED, what a king does, is said aloud and written RAIGNED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be arraigned is to be formally charged in court, called to answer an accusation.

clue.text: Went by car, right to the end — southeastern limit for vehicles

indicators.note: the letter for right is moved from its place to the end of the word

parts.note: drove means travelled in a car

explanation.surface: A motorist drove right to the end of the road, the furthest point cars can go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right to the end' takes R from DROVE and puts it last. DOVER is the Kent port in south-east England where road traffic stops at the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The Channel port in Kent is the south-eastern edge of England, the last stop for road traffic before the sea.

clue.text: Supposedly safe investment said to engender uncomfortable feeling

indicators.note: the word for a safe investment is spoken aloud, giving a different spelling

parts.note: a gilt is a UK government bond, regarded as a very low-risk investment

explanation.surface: A supposedly secure investment is blamed for causing unease.
explanation.walkthrough: GILTS are British government bonds, thought to be among the safest investments.
explanation.definitionFit: Guilt is the troubled emotion of knowing you have done wrong, an uneasy sense of blame.

clue.text: Ex-president is against wrongdoing in one of his states

parts.note: W is the nickname of George W. Bush, former US president
con, as in pros and cons, means against
a sin is a wrongdoing

explanation.surface: A former president, opposed to wrongdoing, campaigns in one of the states he governed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his' refers back to the ex-president: this is one of the US states he led.
explanation.definitionFit: This Midwestern US state is one of the fifty states of the union that a president governs.

clue.text: Wild boar blocking friend by curved path

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit in the middle of the word for friend, blocking it

parts.note: a pal is a friend

indicators.note: a wild version of the word boar is a disordered one

parts.note: by in the sense of per, as in so many a day, gives the letter a

explanation.surface: A wild boar gets in the way of a friend beside a winding track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' gives A because it can mean 'per', and so can 'a', as in so much a day.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the U-shaped curve traced by a thrown object, the path a projectile follows.

clue.text: French leader and British one keeping separated

indicators.note: the number word holds the word for separated inside it

parts.note: one is taken as the word itself
apart means separated

explanation.surface: A French leader and a British one are kept apart from each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' looks like 'leader' but is just the word ONE, which holds APART: B + ON-APART-E.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's surname; he led France as First Consul and then Emperor.

clue.text: Holy man, being glum, starts to describe his unhappiness

parts.note: sad means glum

indicators.note: the first letters of the next three words are taken

explanation.surface: A holy man, feeling down, begins to talk about his misery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' takes D, H and U from 'describe his unhappiness'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadhu is a Hindu ascetic or wandering holy man; this is a variant spelling.

clue.text: Houses in Benin with unpleasant people

parts.note: DY is the international vehicle registration code for Benin
nasties are nasty or unpleasant people

explanation.surface: Homes in the West African country of Benin are shared with disagreeable neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' looks like dwellings, but it means royal families. 'in' looks like a container signal, but here it and 'with' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal house, like the House of Windsor, is a ruling family line.

clue.text: Old-fashioned servant — pick one to take member of family outside

indicators.note: the family member goes around the other two pieces

parts.note: a son is a member of a family
to cull is to pick out or select
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A servant of the old school chooses someone to escort a relative out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to take' is a link and 'outside' is the container signal; 'pick' here means select, not the tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A scullion was a kitchen servant who did the menial work, a term now old-fashioned.

clue.text: There's not any grass for sniffing

parts.note: no means not any
to grass or to sing is to inform on someone to the police

explanation.surface: There's no grass for an animal to sniff about in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' looks like the plant, but it is British slang for informing to the police, as is SING.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosing about is poking the nose into things, sniffing around.

clue.text: Volatile liquid's excellent accompaniment for gin

parts.note: ace means excellent
tonic water is the usual mixer for gin

explanation.surface: A volatile liquid makes a fine partner for gin.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is possessive, matching the adjective: of or relating to acetone, the volatile solvent.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetone is a volatile solvent, and the adjective describes something belonging to or containing it.

clue.text: Think highly of a daughter overcoming predicament

indicators.note: in a down answer, the first pieces sit over the word for predicament

parts.note: a mire is a difficult situation, a predicament

explanation.surface: Someone respects a daughter who has got past a difficult situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overcoming' says A and D come above MIRE in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To admire is to regard with respect and approval, to hold in high esteem.

clue.text: Play down silly dope's fault — not acceptable for the top people

indicators.note: the words are treated as silly, jumbled out of their normal order

parts.note: the possessive here keeps its s as a letter of the fodder

indicators.text: not acceptable for the top people
indicators.note: the letter standing for upper-class acceptability is removed

explanation.surface: Someone tries to make light of a foolish person's error, which the upper classes won't accept.
explanation.walkthrough: U means upper-class, so non-U things are not acceptable to the top people; drop U from DOPESFAULT and 'silly' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To soft-pedal is to make something seem less important, as a pianist mutes the sound with a pedal.

clue.text: Get cut under front of foot

indicators.note: in a down answer, the word for cut sits below the first letter
takes the first letter of the word foot

parts.note: to etch is to cut a design into a surface

explanation.surface: Someone is instructed to be cut beneath the front of the foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' puts ETCH below F in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To fetch is to go and get something and bring it back.

clue.text: Chest will have bit of silver in time of prosperity

indicators.note: the first letter of silver is placed inside the word for prosperous times

parts.note: a boom is a time of economic growth and prosperity

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word silver is taken

explanation.surface: In good times, a chest will contain some silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest' looks like a treasure box, but it is the breast.
explanation.definitionFit: The bosom is the breast or chest of a person.

clue.text: What gives uplift to very old assassin

parts.note: a bra is a garment that lifts and supports

explanation.surface: Something is said to lift the spirits of a very old killer.
explanation.walkthrough: A bravo is an old word for a hired killer, a thug for hire.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravo is an archaic term for a hired thug or killer, a paid murderer.

clue.text: Plant at the back deprived of nitrogen

indicators.note: the chemical symbol is removed from the word for at the back

parts.note: astern means at the back, toward the stern of a ship
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A plant at the back of the garden is short of nitrogen.
explanation.walkthrough: ASTERN, a sailor's word for behind, loses its N.
explanation.definitionFit: The aster is a flowering plant of the daisy family, often called a Michaelmas daisy.

clue.text: Bogus check allowing fifty to escape

indicators.note: the Roman numeral is allowed to escape, so it is removed from the word

parts.note: a limitation is a check or restriction
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A fake cheque lets fifty pounds slip away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'check' suggests a bank cheque, but it means a restraint; LIMITATION loses its L. 'allowing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An imitation is a copy, something fake rather than genuine.

clue.text: One Scot — he eats terrible food snack

indicators.note: the letters of the words are put into a terrible, scrambled order

explanation.surface: A Scotsman is eating some awful food as a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' rearranges ONESCOTHEEATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Grilled cheese on a slice of toast is a classic quick British snack.
